An Accelerated Approach to Time-Sequential 
Production Simulation for Integrated Generation-
Grid-Storage Systems Combining Benders 
Decomposition and Data-Driven Methods 
Jifan Zhang 
School of Electrical Engineering 
Shandong University 
Jinan,China 
1446709380@qq.com
Hengxu Zhang 
School of Electrical Engineering 
Shandong University 
Jinan, China 
zhanghx@sdu.edu.cn 
Wei Li 
NARI Group Corporation (State Grid 
Electric Power Research Institute)  
Nanjing, China 
liwei10@sgepri.sgcc.com.cn  
Abstract—The rapid growth of wind and solar power has 
made electricity system simulations increasingly complex, with 
high-dimensional, tightly interconnected variables that 
overwhelm traditional solution methods. To address this 
challenge, this paper proposes a new  approach that combines 
Benders decomposition with data -driven techniques to 
accelerate large -scale, time -based simulations of integrated 
generation, grid, and storage operations under high renewable 
penetration. The method begins with a detailed analysis of the 
simulation model, which is mathematically structured as a 
large-scale mixed-integer linear program. Using decomposition, 
the model is split into a master problem dealing with discrete 
decisions and subproblems focused on continuous variables. To 
further streamline computation, the framework incorporates a 
pre-screening mechanism based on Gaussian process models. 
This mechanism uses patterns from past solutions to identify 
and remove inactive parts of the feasible region and redundant 
safety constraints, effectively narrowing the search space. A case 
study involving a 90 -node provincial power system shows that 
the proposed method significantly improves computational 
efficiency without compromising accuracy. 
Keywords—Coordinated Time -Series Simulation of 
Generation-Grid-Storage Systems , High-Dimensional Mixed -
Integer Linear Programming, Benders Decomposition, Gaussian 
Process 
I. INTRODUCTION  
As China presses ahead with its “dual carbon” goals, its 
power system is undergoing a rapid transformation toward a 
cleaner, low -carbon structure —one built on multi -energy 
integration and closer coordination between supply and 
demand. The fast-paced expansion of renewable energy has 
made managing the grid more complex. Wind and solar power, 
with their inherent variabili ty and uncertainty, can cause 
issues like frequency instability and voltage deviations. At the 
same time, the different parts of the system —generation, 
transmission, consumption, and storage—are becoming more 
tightly interconnected across both time and space, amplifying 
risks such as power flow disruptions and imbalances between 
supply and demand[1-3]. These challenges highlight the urgent 
need for efficient tools that can assess energy balance risks 
and support the safe and cost-effective operation of the power 
system. 
As renewables take up a growing share of the energy mix, 
grid operations have become increasingly fast-changing and 
dynamic. To maintain system balance, conventional power 
plants are now required to ramp up and down more frequently. 
Time-sequential product ion simulation —an approach that 
captures the temporal dynamics of generation and demand 
using hourly data—has emerged as a key tool for optimizing 
medium- to long -term operations in high -renewable power 
systems. One study [ 4] used this method to optimize t he 
configuration of wind, solar, thermal, and storage systems in 
a direct current near -field setting. Another [ 5] proposed a 
multi-timescale simulation-based approach to assess power 
balance risk. A separate study [6] developed a new frequency 
risk assessment framework grounded in time -sequential 
simulation, offering robust support for the secure and stable 
operation of real-world power systems. 
Time-sequential production simulation must account for 
the operational constraints of multiple types of equipment—
spanning generation, the grid, and energy storage. This 
involves a large number of mixed-integer variables and strong 
intertemporal couplings, resulting in a large -scale mixed -
integer linear programming (MILP) problem. The sheer 
complexity of such models has become a major barrier to 
efficient application in real -world engineering settings. To 
improve solvability, decomposition strategies are of ten 
employed[7], breaking the original problem into smaller, more 
tractable subproblems. These methods preserve modeling 
accuracy while significantly enhancing both computational 
efficiency and practical usability. One study [8], for example, 
applied Benders decomposition to solve the time -sequential 
production simulation model efficiently. 
While decomposition strategies can break down large -
scale mixed -integer programming problems into smaller 
subproblems to reduce complexity, several challenges persist 
in practice. For one, some subproblems still involve high -
dimensional variables and numerous constraints, resulting in 
substantial computational costs per iteration. For another, the 
strong coupling between master and subproblems —and the 
limited efficiency with which cutting planes are transferred 
back to the master problem —can lead to slow converge nce 
and hinder overall optimization performance. Against this 
backdrop, data-driven methods have emerged as a promising 
complement to traditional optimization techniques, 
particularly in the context of complex tasks like operating 
next-generation power systems[9-11]. By mining and learning 
from the wealth of structured data generated during past 
solution processes, predictive models can be developed to 
support variable screening, constraint activation, and solution 
space compression. These models help reduc e the scale of 
subproblems and accelerate convergence —improving the 
overall efficiency and practical applicability of the 
decomposition framework, without sacrificing solution 
quality.

In summary, the paper proposes an accelerated solution framework for time-sequential production simulation in integrated generation–grid–storage systems by combining Benders decomposition with data-driven techniques. The framework first establishes a model that captures the operational characteristics of generation, grid, and storage components, reflecting the system’s dynamic behavior over time. Benders decomposition is then applied to decouple unit commitment from power dispatch, reducing computational complexity. To further alleviate the burden of large-scale subproblems, data-driven methods are introduced for variable screening and solution space reduction, enhancing efficiency. A case study on a provincial power system demonstrates significant improvements in solution speed while maintaining high-quality results. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 introduces the foundational model for time-sequential production simulation. Section 3 presents the Benders decomposition–based optimization framework. Section 4 incorporates data-driven techniques to reduce subproblem dimensionality and improve computational performance. Section 5 concludes with the main findings and future research directions. II. III. REFORMULATION OF THE TIME-SEQUENTIAL SIMULATION MODEL FOR INTEGRATED GENERATION-GRID-STORAGE SYSTEMS A. Analysis of the Characteristics of the Time-Sequential Production Simulation Model Given the high-dimensional, strongly coupled, mixed-integer nature of the time-sequential production simulation model for integrated generation-grid-storage systems, this paper conducts a structural analysis to explore the coupling between unit commitment variables (i.e., integer variables) and generation output variables (i.e., continuous variables). Based on this analysis, a decomposition-based optimization method is proposed, leveraging the structural separation of variable types. The coupling between these variables is primarily reflected in the following three aspects: • Variable activation constraints: The feasibility of generation output variables depends on the activation of unit commitment variables. Specifically, output variables have physical meaning only when the unit is in the “on” state (i.e., the binary status variable equals 1), thereby forming a distinct mixed-integer coupling structure. • Temporal dynamic characteristics: Both commitment and output variables evolve over time and exhibit intertemporal coupling. For example, unit commitment variables are constrained by minimum up/down time logic, while output variables must satisfy sequential power balance and ramping limits—further reinforcing the linkage between the two. • Conditional decoupling: Once unit commitment decisions are fixed in a given optimization round, the associated subproblem involving generation outputs becomes a deterministic linear program with a clear structure, allowing for efficient solution. Based on these structural insights, this paper constructs a decomposition framework that separates the unit commitment master problem from the power dispatch subproblem. The master problem focuses on optimizing combinations of binary startup/shutdown decisions, while the subproblem performs linear optimization of output variables under a fixed unit commitment schedule. B. Reformulation of the Time-Sequential Production Simulation Model Based on Benders Decomposition Benders decomposition, a classical master–subproblem optimization framework, achieves global convergence by decomposing large-scale mixed-integer programming problems into a master problem, a feasibility subproblem, and an optimality subproblem. Through iterative exchanges of cutting planes between the master and subproblems, the method gradually refines the solution space. At this point, the Benders decomposition iteration is terminated.  IV. ACCELERATED SOLUTION OF THE DECOMPOSED TIME-SEQUENTIAL SIMULATION MODEL VIA GAUSSIAN PROCESSES A. Gaussian Process Classifier: Modeling and Training As 0–1 integer variables, unit commitment decisions (i.e., on/off status) can cause a combinatorial explosion in problem size within large-scale mixed-integer linear programming models. Traditional methods such as branch-and-bound often become computational bottlenecks when handling such variables. To address this challenge, this study introduces a predictive model for unit commitment status, trained on historical solution samples, with the goal of pre-screening feasible value spaces and guiding the optimization process probabilistically. By fixing part of the binary variables with high-confidence predictions prior to solving the master problem, computational efficiency can be significantly improved.

Gaussian processes offer strong capabilities in small-sample learning and uncertainty quantification, making them well-suited for classification tasks in complex settings. To enable pre-screening of unit commitment status variables for thermal power units, this study develops a data-driven model based on a Gaussian Process Classifier (GPC). The model is trained on historical solution data accumulated during Benders decomposition iterations, leveraging the strengths of small-sample learning while providing confidence-aware predictions. This allows for both status forecasting and reliability assessment of the predicted outcomes. The overall modeling and training process is outlined as follows: 
 Fig. 2. Schematic of the Data-Driven Approach • Step 1: Construction of Training Samples This study builds the training dataset based on feasible solutions recorded during the Benders decomposition process, extracting their temporal features for model input. Each input feature vector  consists of: [current time index, unit output value, output as a percentage of unit capacity, output as a percentage of total system output, product of output share and total system load shedding, startup indicator, shutdown indicator]. The corresponding output label  is the unit’s on/off status at the same time step in a future iteration, where 1 indicates startup and 0 indicates shutdown. The initial dataset contains 400 samples, and newly generated data from each iteration are continuously added to the historical dataset to ensure broad coverage of representative operating conditions and system states. • Step 2: Kernel Selection and Model Specification The Gaussian Process model in this study is constructed using the commonly adopted squared exponential (SE) kernel. The covariance function is defined as follows:            (18) In this equation,  denotes the signal variance (output scale), and  is the characteristic length scale. Together, they form the set of hyperparameters  for the kernel function. • Step 3: Classifier Training This study employs a maximum marginal likelihood approach to infer the hyperparameters of the Gaussian Process. Specifically, the hyperparameters are learned by maximizing the log marginal likelihood function:    (19) In this equation,  is the covariance matrix of the training samples, computed as ; represents the noise variance, and  is the identity matrix. 
The training process iteratively solves for the hyperparameters  using gradient-based optimization, ultimately determining the optimal kernel function structure. • Step 4: Prediction and Pre-screening Application After completing offline training, the Gaussian Process Classifier is used to predict the posterior probability distribution of unit commitment status for each variable under consideration. For each candidate variable, its corresponding feature vector is fed into the trained model to obtain a probabilistic prediction of the on/off state. Based on the predicted confidence level, a pre-screening rule is applied: if the predicted probability exceeds a specified threshold (or falls below 1− threshold), the variable is classified as a deterministic state and fixed accordingly. Variables falling within the uncertain range are retained as optimization variables and continue to participate in the subsequent optimization process. B. Pre-screening of Variables and Constraints Based on Gaussian Processes Based on the prediction results from the Gaussian Process Classifier, this study proposes a pre-screening strategy targeting both unit commitment variables and redundant constraints in the subproblem. The specific procedures are outlined below. 1) Pre-screening of Unit Commitment Variables Using the confidence scores output by the Gaussian Process Classifier, unit commitment variables are divided into two categories: deterministic and uncertain. A tiered handling strategy is then applied accordingly: • Pre-fixing Deterministic Commitment States The classifier is used to predict the on/off status of thermal units. For those variables with predicted probabilities exceeding a predefined confidence threshold, their commitment status is treated as deterministic and fixed in advance. These fixed variables are incorporated as constants in the subsequent optimization model, thereby reducing the discrete decision space of the master problem. • Probability-Guided Screening of Uncertain States For variables falling within the intermediate probability range—i.e., not confidently classified as on or off—a dynamic weighting coefficient  is constructed based on the predicted uncertainty. This coefficient is designed as a monotonically increasing function of prediction uncertainty and is added to the objective function as a penalty term. By assigning a higher optimization cost to commitment decisions with greater uncertainty, the solver is guided to prioritize candidate solutions with higher overall prediction confidence within the feasible region.  2) Pre-screening of Redundant Subproblem Constraints For units already determined to be offline, their power output variables are mathematically constrained to zero. This allows identification and removal of related constraints that no longer influence the feasible region—such as ramp rate limits or line flow constraints involving those units. These constraints, while present in the model, do not affect the solution and only increase the model’s dimensionality and computational burden. By systematically identifying and

V.CASE STUDY  To verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, a simulation study was conducted using a provincial-level power system as a case example. The network topology of the system is shown in Figure 3, consisting of 90 nodes and 200 transmission lines. The system’s initial configuration is as follows: thermal power capacity of 83.2 GW, wind power capacity of 13 GW, solar PV capacity of 18 GW, energy storage capacity of 2 GW, and a maximum load capacity of 100 GW. 
 Fig. 3. Topology diagram of a provincial case system In this study, the baseline method (hereafter referred to as the original method) is defined as the solver’s default integrated optimization approach. The proposed method, which combines Benders decomposition with data-driven techniques, is used as the improved solution strategy. Simulations are conducted over three different durations—4 days, 7 days, and 30 days—with a time step of 1 hour, resulting in an equivalent daily simulation horizon of 24 hours. Under these varying time scales, the computational time and optimal objective values of the two methods are compared, with results summarized in Tables 1 and 2. original computation time for simulation durations of 4 days, 7 days, and 30 days, respectively. Meanwhile, the relative differences in the optimal objective values were kept within 0.6%, 1.6%, and 2.9%. These results indicate that, under an acceptable level of accuracy loss, the improved method significantly enhances computational efficiency, demonstrating both strong numerical performance and practical engineering applicability. VI.Conclusion The proposed time-sequential simulation approach—integrating Benders decomposition with data-driven techniques—effectively addresses the challenges posed by the high-dimensional and strongly coupled structure of the generation-grid-storage coordination model. Validation using a case study based on a provincial-level power system demonstrates the method’s effectiveness in improving computational efficiency. This approach offers a new pathway for the practical application of time-sequential production simulation in engineering contexts and provides a theoretical foundation for power and energy balance risk assessment in next-generation power systems.
